items: Sam has a red kite; what color is Sam's kite?
Red
Amy went to the park and played on the swings; where did Amy go?
To the park
Ben's dog ran off, so Ben looked under the porch; why did Ben look there?
To find his dog
Mia baked a cake for her grandma's birthday; who was the cake for?
Her grandma
In a story, the cat hid when it heard thunder; what question could you ask about that?
e.g. Why was the cat scared?
Sam got up, ate breakfast, then went to school; what did Sam do first?
He got up
In that story, what did Sam do last?
He went to school
Amy shared her snack with Ben, and the next day he shared his ball with her; what is the lesson?
e.g. When you share, others share with you
In the old fable where a slow tortoise beats a fast hare in a race, what is the lesson?
e.g. Slow and steady wins the race
A boy kept crying "Wolf!" as a joke, so no one came when a real wolf showed up; what is the lesson?
e.g. Tell the truth, or people won't believe you
Who is the character in "Mia fed the ducks at the pond"?
Mia (and the ducks)
Where is the setting in "Mia fed the ducks at the pond"?
At the pond
Ben pulled his sled up the snowy hill; what season is it probably?
Winter
Amy smiled and hugged her new puppy; how is Amy feeling?
Happy
Sam's boat sprang a leak in the middle of the lake; what is the big problem?
e.g. His boat is filling with water
In "The kitten's fur was soft," which word tells how it feels?
Soft
In "The bell went ding-dong," which word tells a sound?
Ding-dong
In "Ben stomped his feet and frowned," how does Ben feel?
Angry or upset
In "The bright sun sparkled on the lake," which words tell what you see?
Bright and sparkled
In "Amy's heart pounded as she tiptoed in the dark," how does Amy feel?
Scared or nervous
Does a book about a talking bear tell a story or give information?
It tells a story
Does a book with real photos of bears and facts about what they eat tell a story or give information?
It gives information
Would you look in a storybook or an information book to find out how tall a giraffe is?
An information book
Which kind of book usually has characters and a problem to solve?
A storybook
What is one thing an information book often has that a storybook does not?
e.g. Real photos, headings, labels, or a glossary
In "I went to the zoo with my dad," is a character telling the story or someone outside it?
A character (the "I" in the story)
In "Sam went to the zoo with his dad," is Sam telling the story or someone else?
Someone else (a narrator)
In a story, the pig says, "Let me in!"; who is talking?
The pig
Which word tells you a character is telling the story, "I" or "she"?
I
In "Mia asked, 'Can I come?' and Ben said, 'Yes!'", who said yes?
Ben
Look at a picture in a storybook together and ask your child to name three things it shows about where the story happens.
Cover the words on a page and have your child tell what is happening from the picture alone, then read to check.
Point to a character in a picture and ask how they feel and which clue in the picture shows it.
Before turning a page, ask your child to use the picture to guess what will happen next.
After reading, have your child draw the main character and tell you two details they noticed in the pictures.
After reading two stories, ask your child which character they would rather be and why.
Read two stories about animals and talk about what was the same and different in their adventures.
Ask your child how a story character's day was like or unlike their own day.
Retell a fairy tale your child knows with a new ending and ask what changed for the characters.
Pick two characters who both had a problem and ask how each one solved it differently.
Take turns reading pages of a simple storybook aloud, helping with tricky words.
Read a short poem together twice, clapping the rhythm the second time.
Have your child read a page aloud to a stuffed animal while you listen.
Let your child read a short story to you and then tell you their favorite part.
Write a four-line rhyming poem together, read it with your child, then let them read it alone.
Frogs live near ponds; where do frogs live?
Near ponds
Bees make honey in a hive; what do bees make?
Honey
Owls hunt at night and sleep in the day; when do owls sleep?
In the day
Penguins can't fly, but they swim very fast; what can penguins do well?
Swim fast
Bears eat a lot in the fall so they can sleep through winter; why do bears eat a lot in the fall?
To get ready to sleep through winter
A page says cats purr, cats nap, and cats like to play; what is it mostly about?
Cats
A book tells how to plant seeds, water them, and give them sun; what is the main topic?
Growing plants from seeds
A page talks about rain, snow, and wind; what is the main topic?
Weather
What is one key detail you might read in a text about fire trucks?
e.g. They carry ladders and hoses
A text says whales are huge, breathe air, and live in the ocean; can you retell two key details?
e.g. Whales are huge and they breathe air
When it rains, the ground gets wet; what makes the ground wet?
The rain
A seed needs water to grow; what happens if it gets no water?
It won't grow
Ice melts when it gets warm; what makes ice melt?
Warmth or heat
A caterpillar makes a cocoon; what does it become next?
A butterfly
How are a tadpole and a frog connected?
A tadpole grows into a frog
In "The puppy was tiny, smaller than my shoe," what does tiny mean?
Very small
In "Bats are nocturnal, so they are awake at night," what does nocturnal mean?
Awake at night
In "The giraffe stretched its neck to reach the high leaves," what does reach mean?
To stretch out to touch or get something
What could you ask when you don't know a word in a book?
e.g. What does this word mean?
In "The squirrel stores nuts for winter," what does stores mean?
Saves or keeps them for later
Where is the title of a book usually found?
On the front cover
Which part of a book lists the chapters and their page numbers?
The table of contents
What does a heading on a page tell you?
What that part of the page is about
Where in a book can you look up what hard words mean?
The glossary
On a tablet or website, where does a little house icon usually take you?
To the home page or home screen
The words say "This is a frog" and the picture shows a green frog; what did the picture add?
That the frog is green
The words say "Zebras have stripes"; what could a picture show that the words don't?
e.g. That the stripes are black and white
The words say "The ant carried food" and the picture shows a leaf; how do you know it was a leaf?
From the picture
A page says "Snakes eat eggs" next to a photo of a snake; did you learn what snakes eat from the words or the picture?
The words
A drawing of a bird has an arrow with the label "beak"; what does the label tell you?
Which part of the bird is the beak
Read a nonfiction page together and ask your child what the picture teaches that the words don't say.
Look at a photo of an animal together and list three facts you can learn just by looking.
Find a labeled picture in a book or online and have your child use the labels to explain the parts.
Draw a simple map of your street together and use it to talk about where things are.
Look at a recipe with step photos and have your child explain each step from the pictures.
"Wear a helmet because it keeps your head safe"; what reason does the author give?
It keeps your head safe
"Dogs are good pets because they love to play"; why does the author think dogs are good pets?
They love to play
"Eat your vegetables; they help you grow strong"; what reason does the author give?
They help you grow strong
"Recycling is good because it makes less trash"; why does the author say recycling is good?
It makes less trash
"Bats are helpful because they eat bugs and spread seeds"; how many reasons does the author give?
2 (they eat bugs and spread seeds)
Read two short pages about the same animal and ask your child to name one fact both of them shared.
Look at two different pictures of the same animal and talk about what is the same and what is different.
Read two sets of steps for making the same snack and compare how they are alike and different.
Read a short text and watch a short video on the same topic, then ask which one taught something new.
After reading two texts about weather, ask your child to find one fact in one that wasn't in the other.
Read a short nonfiction page together, taking turns reading each sentence.
Have your child read the steps of a recipe aloud while you cook together.
Read a short fact page about an animal and ask your child to tell you one new fact.
Walk around the house reading signs, labels, and lists together.
Write a short note with three facts about your family and have your child read it aloud.
What kind of letter starts every sentence?
A capital (uppercase) letter
What mark often ends a telling sentence?
A period
What mark ends a question?
A question mark
In "the dog ran." what needs fixing?
The first word needs a capital: The
What mark could end "Wow, look at that"?
An exclamation point
What is the first sound in "map"?
Does "cake" have a long a or a short a sound?
A long a
What word do these sounds make: /s/ /t/ /o/ /p/?
Stop
What is the middle sound in "sit"?
/i/ (short i)
How many sounds are in "frog"?
What sound do the letters s and h make together?
/sh/, as in ship
What word do you get when you add an e to the end of "cap"?
Cape
What sound do the letters ee make in "tree"?
A long e sound
How many syllables are in "rabbit"?
2 (rab-bit)
What ending do you add to "jump" to make "jumped"?
-ed

Take turns reading lines of a story in different character voices to practice expression.
When your child misreads a word, ask "Does that make sense?" and let them reread the sentence.

Have your child read one sentence as a question, then as an exclamation, then in a normal voice.
Ask your child to write one sentence about their favorite food and one reason why.

Help your child write three sentences telling how to brush your teeth.
Ask your child to make an "All About Me" page with a first sentence, some facts, and an ending.

Ask your child to draw a picture and write two sentences about a fun trip to the park.
Help your child write a short story about a pet with a beginning, a middle, and an end.
Have your child write about their weekend and add one detail about how they felt.
Ask your child to finish a story that starts "One morning, Sam found a box..." with a clear ending.
Read your child's writing back to them and ask, "What else could you add?"

Help your child check that every sentence in their writing is about the same topic.
Help your child type a short sentence about their day on a computer or tablet.
Use a phone to record your child reading a sentence they wrote, then play it back together.
Help your child type and send a short message to a relative.
Let your child take a photo and type one sentence that describes it.
Type a short story together, taking turns writing each sentence.
Look up how to make a sandwich together and write the steps in order.
Pick an animal, find three facts together in a book or online, and write them down.
Watch a short how-to video together and write the steps as a numbered list.
Write instructions for washing hands together, numbering each step, then follow them to test.
Make a mini poster together about a topic your child picks, with a title and two facts.

Look at a family photo and help your child write what happened that day.
Ask "What do plants need?" and help your child find the answer in a book or online.
Ask your child to remember three things from a recent outing and make a short list.
After a walk, help your child write down two things they saw or heard.
At dinner, take turns talking about your day, with each person waiting until the other finishes.
Play "pass the spoon," where only the person holding the spoon may talk.
Have a chat where your child responds to what you just said before adding their own idea.
Read a page together and invite your child to ask one question about anything confusing.

Read a short story aloud and ask your child three questions about it.

Give a quick weather report out loud and ask your child what they should wear.

Ask your child to describe their bedroom using three details.

Ask your child to tell you about a fun day and how they felt.
Have your child describe a family member by what they look like and what they like to do.
Ask your child to describe the weather outside using colors, sounds, and feelings.
Have your child draw their favorite place and use the drawing to describe it to you.
Ask your child to draw a face showing how they feel today and explain why.
Have your child draw the steps of their morning routine and talk you through them.

When your child answers with one word, gently ask them to say it as a full sentence.

What is the word for more than one cat?
Cats
Which is right, "He hop" or "He hops"?
He hops
What word fits: "Yesterday I ___ home" (walk)?
Walked
What word fits: "Tomorrow I ___ walk home"?
Will
Can you join "I like milk" and "I like juice" into one sentence using "and"?
e.g. I like milk and juice.
Should "mia" start with a capital letter when it is a girl's name?
Yes: Mia
What mark goes at the end of "Can you help me"?
A question mark
How do you spell "said"?
S-A-I-D
Where does the comma go when you write the date May 5 2026?
After the 5: May 5, 2026
Where do the commas go in "I like red blue and green"?
After red and blue: I like red, blue, and green.
What is the root word in "looking"?
Look
Can you name two other forms of the word "jump"?
e.g. Jumps, jumped, jumping
What does "un" mean in "unhappy"?
Not (not happy)
What does "redo" mean?
To do again
In "Ben was so sleepy that he yawned," what does yawned mean?
Opened his mouth wide because he was tired
Which word doesn't belong: red, blue, sock, green?
Sock (the others are colors)
A duck is a bird that swims; what is a cow?
e.g. A farm animal that moos and gives milk
Can you name a place at home that is cozy?
e.g. My bed or the couch
Which word means bigger, "large" or "gigantic"?
Gigantic
Which is a quick look, "glance" or "stare"?
Glance
Can you finish this: "I wore a coat because..."?
e.g. it was cold
Which word joins these: "I like apples ___ I like pears"?
And
Which fits, "but" or "so": "It was raining, ___ we stayed inside"?
So
Which fits, "and" or "but": "I wanted cake, ___ it was all gone"?
But
Which word fits: "Would you like milk ___ juice?"
Or
"Sam lost his red hat at the park." Who lost something?
Sam
"Amy fed her cat after school." When did Amy feed her cat?
After school
"Mia hid the gift under her bed." Where did Mia hide the gift?
Under her bed
"Ben ran home because it started to rain." Why did Ben run home?
Because it started to rain
"The fox could not reach the grapes, so he walked away grumbling." How did the fox feel?
e.g. Grumpy or upset, because he couldn't reach the grapes
In "The Tortoise and the Hare," who wins the race?
The tortoise
What is the lesson of "The Tortoise and the Hare"?
e.g. Slow and steady wins the race – don't show off or give up.
In "The Boy Who Cried Wolf," why did no one come to help at the end?
He had lied before, so nobody believed him.
What is the lesson of "The Boy Who Cried Wolf"?
e.g. Tell the truth, or people won't believe you.
A tiny mouse frees a lion from a net; what is the lesson of that fable?
e.g. Even small friends can be a big help, so be kind to everyone.
Sam drops his ice cream cone; how might he feel?
e.g. Sad or upset
Amy's kite gets stuck in a tree; what could she do?
e.g. Ask a grown-up to help get it down
When the wolf comes to the brick house, what does the third little pig do?
He stays inside and keeps the wolf out (and is safe).
What do the first two pigs do when the wolf blows their houses down?
They run to their brother's brick house.
Ben loses a race but shakes the winner's hand; what does that show about him?
e.g. He is a good sport and kind.
Which word rhymes with "cat": dog, hat, or cup?
hat
What sound repeats in "Silly Sam sings songs"?
The "s" sound (that's called alliteration)
Finish the rhyme: "The bug sat on a ___."
e.g. rug, mug, or jug
In "Hickory, dickory, dock, the mouse ran up the clock," which words rhyme?
Hickory and dickory; dock and clock
Why do poems and songs often repeat a line?
e.g. It makes a beat and helps you remember the important part.
Which part of a story usually tells us who the characters are?
The beginning
What usually happens in the middle of a story?
A problem happens and the characters try to fix it.
What does the ending of a story usually do?
It solves the problem and wraps things up.
How does "Goldilocks and the Three Bears" begin?
e.g. Goldilocks goes into the bears' house while they are out.
How does "Goldilocks and the Three Bears" end?
The bears come home and find her, and she runs away.

Take turns reading the talking parts aloud – you read one character and your child reads the other.
Pause during a story and ask, "How does this character feel, and does the other one feel the same?"

Act out a short scene with toys, giving each toy its own voice and its own opinion.

Point to a character's face in a picture and talk about how they feel.
Look at a picture and ask, "Where and when do you think this story happens?"
Read a page without showing the picture, then show it and talk about what it added.
Flip through a new book's pictures first and predict what the story will be about.

Compare two versions of a story and name one thing that's different, like the setting or the ending.
Draw a two-column chart showing how two versions of a story start and end.
Ask your child which version of a story they liked better, and why.
Find a folktale from another country at the library and compare it with one you already know.
Read a picture book or short chapter together for 10 minutes, taking turns page by page.
Read a short poem aloud twice, then talk about your favorite line.
After reading, ask your child to tell the story in three sentences: beginning, middle, and end.
Stop partway through a story and ask your child to predict what happens next.
Let your child pick a library book and read the first chapter aloud to you.
"Bees make honey in a hive." What do bees make?
Honey
"Bears sleep in caves all winter." Where do bears sleep?
In caves
"Bears sleep in caves all winter." When do they sleep?
All winter
"Frogs have sticky tongues to catch bugs." Why are frogs' tongues sticky?
To catch bugs
"Firefighters spray water to put out fires." Who puts out fires, and how?
Firefighters, by spraying water
A book has pages about lions, zebras, and giraffes; what is its main topic?
e.g. Wild animals of Africa
A text has parts called "Rain," "Snow," and "Hail"; what is the main topic?
Weather
A paragraph tells what a dog eats, where it sleeps, and how to walk it; what is it about?
Taking care of a dog
A book has paragraphs about roots, stems, and leaves; what is the main topic?
Parts of a plant
In a book about the moon, one paragraph is all about astronauts; what is that paragraph's focus?
The people who went to the moon
To make a sandwich, what do you do after you take out the bread?
e.g. Spread the filling on it
A seed gets water and sun; what happens next?
It sprouts and grows into a plant.
Why does an ice cube melt when you leave it in the sun?
The sun warms it up.
Put in order: the chick hatches, the hen lays an egg, the chick grows up.
The hen lays an egg, the chick hatches, the chick grows up.
Water turns into steam and the steam cools high in the sky; what forms?
Clouds (and then rain)
"A cub is a baby bear." What is a cub?
A baby bear
"A pond is a frog's habitat." What does habitat mean?
The place where an animal lives
"An herbivore eats only plants." What does an herbivore eat?
Only plants
"The desert is dry and gets very little rain." What is a desert?
A dry place with very little rain
"A caterpillar changes into a butterfly." What does changes into mean?
Turns into or becomes
What do we call the words under a picture that tell about it?
A caption
Where near the front of a book can you find the chapters and their page numbers?
The table of contents
Why are some words in a science book printed in bold?
They are important words, often explained in the glossary.
Where at the back of a book can you find what a hard word means?
The glossary
Which part at the back of a book lists topics in ABC order with page numbers?
The index
Why would someone write a recipe?
To explain how to make a food
What is the purpose of a sign that says "Wet Floor"?
To warn people so they don't slip
A text is called "How Do Birds Fly?" What question does the author want to answer?
How birds fly
Why might an author write a book all about sharks?
e.g. To teach readers facts about sharks
A text tells what a farm looks, sounds, and smells like; does it explain, describe, or answer a question?
It describes.
Why might a book about the body show a picture of a skeleton?
To show where the bones are
What does a map in a book help you understand?
Where places are
How do labels on a diagram help a reader?
They name the parts so you can see what each one is.
Why do building instructions often have a picture for each step?
So you can see exactly what to do.
A life-cycle diagram has arrows between pictures; what do the arrows show?
The order things happen in
"Dogs make good pets because they are loyal." What reason does the author give?
They are loyal.
"Eat vegetables, because they help you grow strong." What is the reason?
They help you grow strong.
Which reason supports "Recycling is good": it helps the Earth, or it's a long word?
It helps the Earth.
What is a good reason for the point "Wear a helmet when you bike"?
e.g. A helmet protects your head if you fall.
Can you give two reasons that support "Exercise is good for you"?
e.g. It makes your heart strong and gives you energy.

Draw two overlapping circles on paper and sort facts from two texts into same and different.
Ask your child which of two books explained a topic better, and why.
Watch a short kids' science video and read a page on the same topic, then compare the main points.

Read the instructions for a board game together before you play.
Read the label on a food package together and find two facts.
Read a short kids' news story and talk about who, what, where, and why.
Does "cap" have a short "a" or a long "a" sound?
Short "a"
What word do you get if you add an "e" to the end of "cap"?
"cape" – now the "a" is long
Which two letters make the long "e" sound in "team"?
e and a ("ea")
Which letter is silent in "know"?
The "k"
In "replay," what is the prefix and what does the word mean?
"re-"; it means to play again
Read the same short page aloud three times and notice how it gets smoother each time.

When your child misreads a word, ask "Does that make sense?" and let them reread the sentence.

Have your child read a familiar page for one minute, then try again with fewer mistakes.

Read their writing aloud and ask if any part sounds confusing, then fix it together.

Use voice typing to say a few sentences, then fix any mistakes together.
Type a family to-do list together and save it to share.

Look out the window each morning for a week and record if it is sunny, cloudy, or rainy.

What is the plural of "foot"?
feet
What do we call a group of sheep: a flock or a pack?
A flock
Yesterday I ___ you a story: what is the past tense of "tell"?
told
Fill in the blank: "I made it all by ___."
myself
Which is correct: "She ran quick" or "She ran quickly"?
"She ran quickly" (quickly tells how she ran)
Which needs a capital letter: thanksgiving or turkey?
Thanksgiving – it's a holiday
Should the word texas start with a capital letter?
Yes – Texas is the name of a place
In a letter, what punctuation goes after "Dear Grandma"?
A comma
What is the short way to write "do not"?
don't
How do you write that a ball belongs to Sam?
Sam's ball – with an apostrophe before the s
Which is more formal: "Hi!" or "Good morning"?
"Good morning"
Is a quick text to a friend usually formal or informal?
Informal
Would you say "Hey, dude!" to the school principal?
No – you'd say something formal like "Good morning."
How could you say "Gimme that" in a polite, formal way?
e.g. "May I have that, please?"
How would you start a thank-you letter to your teacher?
e.g. "Dear Ms. Lee,"
What does "unhappy" mean?
Not happy
What does "retell" mean?
To tell again
What is a "bookshelf"?
A shelf for books
If you know the word "help," what is a "helper"?
Someone who helps
In "The bat flew out of the cave," is the bat an animal or a baseball bat?
An animal – it flew out of a cave
Can you name a food that is crunchy?
e.g. carrots, apples, or crackers
Can you name something that is sticky?
e.g. honey or glue
Which is bigger: something large or something huge?
Something huge
Which word is the strongest: glad, happy, or thrilled?
thrilled
Put these in order from gentlest to strongest: hurl, toss, throw.
toss, throw, hurl
What is a describing word for the sky today?
e.g. blue, cloudy, or bright
What is a better word for "big" in "a big elephant"?
e.g. huge, enormous, or giant
Finish with a word ending in -ly: "The puppy ran ___."
e.g. quickly or happily
Finish this: "When my friends are happy, that makes me ___."
e.g. happy too
Can you tell how a turtle moves, using a describing word?
e.g. "The turtle moves slowly."
Sam put on his boots because it was snowing. Why did Sam wear boots?
Because it was snowing.
Mia dropped her ice cream and started to cry. How did Mia feel, and what tells you?
Sad – she started to cry.
Ben looked under the bed and found his lost shoe. Where was the shoe?
Under the bed.
Amy whispered so she wouldn't wake the baby. Why did she whisper?
So the baby would keep sleeping.
The dog barked at the door, and Sam ran to open it. What do you think was at the door?
e.g. a visitor – the dog barked at the door.
A tortoise beats a fast but lazy hare in a race. What is the lesson?
e.g. Slow and steady wins the race.
A boy keeps shouting 'Wolf!' as a joke, so no one helps when a real wolf comes. What is the lesson?
e.g. If you lie, people won't believe you, even when you tell the truth.
An ant works all summer while a grasshopper plays, and in winter the ant has food. What is the moral?
e.g. Work hard now and plan ahead.
A tiny mouse frees a lion from a net after the lion spared him. What is the message?
e.g. Small friends can be a big help; kindness is repaid.
How can you tell what a fable's lesson is?
e.g. Look at what happens to the characters because of their choices.
Sam shared his lunch with a new kid. What word describes Sam?
e.g. kind or generous
Mia practiced piano every day so she could play at the show. What did Mia want?
To play well at the show.
Ben was nervous, so he hid behind his mom. How did his feeling change what he did?
He hid instead of saying hello, because he was nervous.
Amy forgot to close the gate, and the dog ran out. How did Amy's action change the story?
The dog got out, so now they have to find it.
A character keeps trying after failing three times. What trait does that show?
e.g. determined or brave
What does 'it's raining cats and dogs' really mean?
It's raining very hard.
If someone has 'butterflies in their stomach', how do they feel?
Nervous.
What does 'break a leg' mean when said before a show?
Good luck.
Is 'Sam ran as fast as a cheetah' literal or nonliteral?
Nonliteral – it means he ran very fast.
What does 'Mia's room was a pigpen' mean?
Her room was very messy.
What do we call a group of lines in a poem?
A stanza.
What do we call one part of a chapter book?
A chapter.
What is a part of a play called?
A scene (or an act).
In a story, why is chapter 1 important for chapter 2?
e.g. It introduces the characters and problem that chapter 2 builds on.
In a play, what are the lines in parentheses telling actors what to do called?
Stage directions.
If a story says 'I ran to the park', who is telling it?
A character in the story – the narrator (first person).
If a story says 'She ran to the park', is the narrator in the story?
No – it's told by an outside narrator (third person).
The wolf in a story thinks the pigs are being rude. Do you agree?
e.g. No, I think the wolf was the rude one.
A character thinks rainy days are boring. Is that your opinion too?
e.g. No – I like splashing in puddles.
Why might a narrator and a reader feel differently about a character?
e.g. They notice different things or have different experiences.

'Bees make honey from flower nectar.' What do bees use to make honey?
Flower nectar.
'Frogs lay eggs in water. The eggs hatch into tadpoles.' What hatches from frog eggs?
Tadpoles.
'Bears sleep through winter because food is hard to find.' Why do bears sleep in winter?
Because food is hard to find.
'The Moon has no air, so astronauts wear space suits.' Why do astronauts wear suits on the Moon?
Because there is no air.
'Penguins can't fly, but they are fast swimmers.' What can penguins do well?
Swim fast.
'Dogs help people. Some guide people who can't see. Some help find lost hikers.' What is the main idea?
Dogs help people.
'Plants need sun. They need water. They need soil.' What is the main idea?
Plants need certain things to grow.
Main idea: 'Recycling helps Earth.' Give one detail that could support it.
e.g. It means less trash goes into the ground.
'Owls hunt at night. They have big eyes and hear very well.' What details show owls are good night hunters?
Big eyes and very good hearing.
What is the difference between a main idea and a detail?
The main idea is what it's mostly about; details tell more about it.
'First, crack the egg. Next, stir it. Then cook it.' What comes after stirring?
Cooking it.
'Heavy rain fell, so the river flooded.' What caused the flood?
Heavy rain.
A caterpillar makes a chrysalis. What happens after that?
It turns into a butterfly.
'When water gets very cold, it freezes into ice.' What is the cause and what is the effect?
Cause: very cold; effect: water turns to ice.
Put in order: the seed sprouts, you plant the seed, a flower blooms.
Plant the seed, the seed sprouts, a flower blooms.
In a science book, what does 'habitat' mean?
The natural home of an animal or plant.
What does 'predator' mean?
An animal that hunts other animals for food.
What is a 'liquid'?
Something that flows, like water or milk.
In a history book, what does 'colony' mean?
A place settled and ruled by people from another country.
What does 'evaporate' mean?
To turn from a liquid into a gas, like a puddle drying up.
Where in a book can you find the chapter names and page numbers?
The table of contents.
Where in a book would you look to find what a bold word means?
The glossary.
Where in a book can you find every page that talks about frogs?
The index.
What is a caption?
The words under a picture that explain it.
When searching online about whales, what key word would you type?
e.g. whales (or 'what do whales eat')
An author writes 'Recess should be longer.' What is the author's opinion?
Recess should be longer.
An author says snakes are scary. Do you agree, and why?
e.g. No – most snakes are harmless.
An author says 'Winter is the best season.' What is your point of view?
e.g. I think summer is best because school is out.
How can you tell an author's point of view in a text?
e.g. Look for opinion words like best, should, or I think.
An author says kids should not have pets. What might your point of view be?
e.g. Kids can learn responsibility from pets.

'Cats like to nap. Dogs, however, like to play.' Is that comparing or showing cause?
Comparing (showing a difference).
'It didn't rain, so the plants dried out.' What connection is this?
Cause and effect.
What words show order in a set of steps?
e.g. first, next, then, finally
'Both frogs and toads lay eggs.' What does 'both' show?
How two things are alike (comparison).
Why might a paragraph start with 'Because of this'?
It shows the paragraph is an effect of what came before.

Read a short article about an animal, then ask your child to teach you three facts.
What does 're-' mean in 'reread'?
Again – read it again.
What does 'un-' mean in 'unhappy'?
Not – not happy.
What does '-ful' mean in 'helpful'?
Full of – full of help.
How many syllables are in 'butterfly'?
3 (but-ter-fly).
What does '-less' mean in 'careless'?
Without – without care.

In 'The dog ran fast', which word is the verb?
ran
What is the plural of 'child'?
children
What is the past tense of 'run'?
ran
Which is correct: 'She go to school' or 'She goes to school'?
She goes to school.
Fill in: Ben is tall, Sam is taller, and Mia is the ___.
tallest
Which words get capital letters in the title 'the big red barn'?
The Big Red Barn
Where does the comma go in 'Dallas Texas'?
After Dallas: Dallas, Texas
How do you show who owns the bike that belongs to Sam?
Sam's bike
What is 'cry' + '-es'?
cries
How do you spell 'happy' + '-ness'?
happiness
Which is more exciting: 'The dog walked' or 'The dog raced'?
The dog raced.
Give a stronger word for 'big'.
e.g. huge, giant, enormous
Give a better word for 'said' if someone is very happy.
e.g. cheered or laughed
Is 'gonna' used more in speaking or in writing?
Speaking – in writing use 'going to'.
How could you change 'It was a nice day' to make it more vivid?
e.g. It was a warm, sunny day.
What does 'unkind' mean?
Not kind.
What does 'preheat' mean?
To heat before.
What does 'disagree' mean?
To not agree.
'Bat' can mean an animal. What else can it mean?
A stick used to hit a ball.
'Sam's companion walked with him.' Using 'company', what is a companion?
A friend who goes with you.
What does 'take steps' really mean in 'take steps to stay safe'?
Do things to stay safe.
Name someone who is helpful and what they do.
e.g. A firefighter puts out fires.
Which is more sure: 'I knew' or 'I wondered'?
I knew.
Put in order from least sure to most sure: believed, wondered, knew.
wondered, believed, knew
What is a word for a person who is friendly?
e.g. kind, warm, outgoing
In 'After dinner we played', when did they play?
After dinner.
What word tells where: 'The cat hid under the bed'?
under
What word means the opposite of 'before'?
after
Use 'meanwhile' in a sentence.
e.g. Mom cooked; meanwhile, I set the table.
What does 'beside' mean in 'Amy sat beside Ben'?
Next to.
Sam slammed the door and stomped up the stairs. How do you think Sam feels, and which details tell you?
Angry or upset - he slammed the door and stomped.
Mia grabbed her umbrella and rain boots before going out. What can you infer about the weather?
It is raining or about to rain - she took an umbrella and boots.
Ben's hands shook as he walked onto the stage, and he kept clearing his throat. What can you infer?
He is nervous - his hands shook and he kept clearing his throat.
The story says, "Amy's plate was empty in two minutes, and she asked for more." What can you infer, and what is your evidence?
She liked the food or was very hungry - she ate fast and asked for more.
The garden was full of weeds, the gate hung off one hinge, and the windows were dusty. What can you infer about the house, and which details prove it?
Nobody has looked after it for a long time - weeds, a broken gate and dusty windows.
A tortoise beats a fast hare in a race because the hare stops to nap. What is a theme of this story?
Slow and steady wins the race; don't be overconfident.
A boy keeps crying "Wolf!" as a joke, so no one believes him when a real wolf comes. What is the theme?
If you lie, people won't believe you even when you tell the truth.
An ant works all summer storing food while a grasshopper plays. In winter the grasshopper is hungry. What is the theme?
Work hard and plan ahead.
Summarize this in one sentence: Mia lost her dog, put up posters, searched all weekend, and a neighbor finally called to say he'd found it.
e.g. Mia worked hard to find her lost dog, and a neighbor helped bring it home.
A mouse frees a trapped lion by chewing the net, after the lion once spared the mouse. What is a theme, and which details show it?
Even small friends can be a big help; kindness is repaid - the tiny mouse saves the lion who spared him.
Ben shares his lunch with a new kid who forgot his. What word describes Ben, and what action shows it?
Kind or generous - he shared his lunch.
Amy says, "I'll never try that again - it's too hard!" What does this show about how she feels?
Frustrated or ready to give up.
A story says the forest was dark, cold, and silent except for an owl's hoot. What kind of setting is this, and what details create it?
Spooky or scary - dark, cold, silent, an owl hooting.
Sam thinks, "I should tell the truth, but I'll get in trouble." What does this thought show about him?
He is torn - he wants to be honest but is afraid of the consequences.
Mia practices piano every day, even on weekends, and asks her teacher for harder songs. Describe Mia using two traits and evidence.
e.g. Hardworking and determined - she practices daily and wants harder songs.
In "Sam gobbled his dinner," what does "gobbled" mean?
Ate it very quickly.
Hercules was a hero of great strength. What is a "Herculean task"?
A job that needs huge strength or effort.
In Greek myths, Pandora opened a box that let out troubles. What does "opening Pandora's box" mean?
Starting something that causes lots of unexpected problems.
Achilles was a hero who could only be hurt on his heel. What is someone's "Achilles' heel"?
Their weak spot.
In "The wind whispered through the trees," what does "whispered" tell you about the wind?
It was soft and quiet, gently blowing.
What do we call the groups of lines in a poem?
Stanzas (or verses).
In a play, what are stage directions?
Instructions that tell actors how to move or speak, usually in brackets or italics.
What is the list of characters at the start of a play called?
The cast of characters (cast list).
Name one way a poem usually looks different from a story written in prose.
e.g. A poem is in short lines and stanzas; prose is in sentences and paragraphs.
What is the rhythm or meter of a poem?
The pattern of strong and weak beats in the lines.
"I ran to the bus stop." Is this first person or third person?
First person - it uses "I".
"She ran to the bus stop." Is this first person or third person?
Third person - it uses "she".
Which words are clues that a story is told in first person?
I, me, my, we, us, our.
In a first-person story, who is telling the story?
A character inside the story.
Why might a third-person narrator be able to tell you more than a first-person narrator?
They can tell what several characters think and do, not just one person's view.
Read a short scene from a story, then act it out together, following exactly what the words say characters do.
Listen to a story read aloud, then talk about how the reader's voice showed each character's feelings.
After reading a story you have also seen as a movie or show, name one thing the screen version kept the same and one it changed.
Read a description of a character, then each draw them and compare which details from the text you both used.
Read a short play script aloud together and follow the stage directions, then talk about how they change the scene.
Many stories have a hero who goes on a long journey to find something. What is this pattern called?
A quest.
Name a common theme found in fairy tales and myths from many countries.
e.g. Good against evil; kindness is rewarded; cleverness beats strength.
Lots of cultures have a Cinderella-type story. What usually happens to the kind, mistreated girl at the end?
She is rewarded - often she marries a prince or finds happiness.
In many folk tales a small animal tricks a bigger one. What lesson does this pattern often teach?
Brains can beat strength.
If two myths from different cultures both explain why the sun moves across the sky, what is similar and what might be different?
e.g. Same topic or purpose; different characters, gods, or details.
Share 10 minutes of reading a chapter book, taking turns reading pages aloud.
Read a short poem together twice and talk about what picture it puts in your head.
After your child reads a chapter, ask them to tell you what happened and what they think will happen next.
Read a short play scene aloud together, each taking a different part.
When a sentence is tricky, reread it together and talk through what it means.
A text says "Bats sleep during the day and hunt at night." When do bats look for food?
At night.
A text says most desert animals rest in burrows during the hot day. What can you infer about why?
To stay cool and avoid the heat.
"Frogs lay eggs in water, and tadpoles live in water until they grow legs." What can you infer about where frogs need to live?
Near water.
A text says a town built a dam after floods damaged homes three years in a row. Why did they build the dam, and what detail tells you?
To stop flooding - floods damaged homes three years running.
A text says honeybees visit flowers and carry pollen to other flowers, which helps plants make seeds. What can you infer would happen to some plants without bees?
They might not make seeds or fruit, so fewer plants would grow.
A paragraph says dogs help people by guiding the blind, finding lost hikers, and herding sheep. What is the main idea?
Dogs help people in many ways.
Name one key detail that supports the main idea that dogs help people.
e.g. They guide blind people, find lost hikers, or herd sheep.
A text explains that recycling saves trees, saves energy, and keeps trash out of landfills. What is the main idea?
Recycling is good for the environment.
What is the difference between a main idea and a detail?
The main idea is what the whole text is mostly about; details are facts that support it.
Summarize in one sentence: Penguins can't fly, but they swim very fast, dive deep, and use their wings like flippers.
e.g. Penguins can't fly but are excellent swimmers.
A text says ice melts when it gets warm. What happens and why?
The ice turns to water because heat warms it.
A recipe says to mix the flour and eggs before adding milk. What step comes first?
Mixing the flour and eggs.
A text says the colonists were angry about taxes on tea, so they dumped tea into the harbor. Why did they dump the tea?
Because they were angry about the tea tax.
A text says plants need sunlight to make food, so a plant left in a dark closet will die. Explain why.
Without sunlight it can't make food.
A text explains that volcanoes erupt when melted rock builds pressure underground and pushes up. What causes the eruption?
Pressure from melted rock (magma) pushing up from underground.
In science, what does "habitat" mean?
The natural home of an animal or plant.
What is "evaporation"?
When a liquid, like water, turns into a gas (vapor).
In social studies, what is a "colony"?
A place settled and ruled by people from another country.
"The predator, a hawk, swooped down on the mouse." Using clues, what is a predator?
An animal that hunts and eats other animals.
What does "erosion" mean in a text about rivers and rocks?
The slow wearing away of land or rock by water, wind, or ice.
A text tells what happened in 1800, then 1850, then 1900. What structure is this?
Chronology (time order).
A text explains how frogs and toads are alike and different. What structure is this?
Compare and contrast.
A text says heavy rain fell, so the river flooded. What structure is this?
Cause and effect.
